items.stem:
Source B
By 1938 the Chiefs of Staff had warned that Britain could not prevent Germany from overrunning Czechoslovakia, and that a war at that time might lead to the bombing of London with heavy casualties.
— Summary of the Chiefs of Staff report “The Military Implications of German Aggression against Czechoslovakia”, March 1938 (paraphrased)

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source B for an historian studying the Munich Agreement and appeasement. [3]
items.answer: Value: It is official military advice to the Cabinet, showing the strategic constraints on Chamberlain. Limitations: It reflects the cautious assumptions of the military, which may have exaggerated German air power.
items.markingKey: Value: It is official military advice to the Cabinet, showing the strategic constraints on Chamberlain. Limitations: It reflects the cautious assumptions of the military, which may have exaggerated German air power. Award up to [3]: origin, purpose and content must each be referred to and linked to value or limitation for the stated enquiry. items.stem: "Primary sources are always more valuable than secondary sources for a historical investigation." With reference to specific examples, discuss. [15]
items.answer: Neither type is inherently more valuable; value depends on the question and the critical use made of the source.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 essay. items.stem: Explain the difference between the value of a source and the relevance of a source.
items.answer: Relevance explains why the source relates to the research question; value is the analysis of how its origin, purpose and content make it useful as evidence for the question.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the ExComm tapes are the most valuable source for understanding the Cuban Missile Crisis? [15]
items.answer: The tapes are uniquely valuable for US decision-making but must be combined with Soviet and Cuban sources.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that it is impossible for historians to be objective?
items.answer: Absolute objectivity is impossible, but rigorous method makes some interpretations more reliable than others.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: selection of evidence and questions (Carr); national perspectives on events such as Nanjing; historians’ contexts shape interpretations. Arguments against: rules of evidence and corroboration (Elton); peer review and debate; some facts are not disputed. Supported judgement: Absolute objectivity is impossible, but rigorous method makes some interpretations more reliable than others. Markbands (10 marks): Use the IB Paper 2/3 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – clearly focused, well structured, in-depth accurate knowledge supporting critical analysis, perspectives evaluated, reasoned conclusion; middle band – mostly accurate knowledge, some analysis but partly narrative; lower band – limited understanding of the demands, mainly description.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Section 1 of the IA"?
options: Identification and evaluation of sources: the student states the research question, explains the relevance of two sources and analyses their value and limitations with reference to origin, purpose and content (6 marks, about 500 words)
The processes historians use, including selecting and evaluating sources, corroboration, constructing interpretations and dealing with gaps or bias in evidence
Reflection: the student reflects on what the investigation revealed about the methods used by historians and the challenges they face (4 marks, about 400 words)
Examining evidence and arguments, explaining their significance and weighing them to reach a judgement
items.answer: Identification and evaluation of sources: the student states the research question, explains the relevance of two sources and analyses their value and limitations with reference to origin, purpose and content (6 marks, about 500 words)
items.markingKey: A. "Section 1 of the IA" is identification and evaluation of sources: the student states the research question, explains the relevance of two sources and analyses their value and limitations with reference to origin, purpose and content (6 marks, about 500 words).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Section 2 of the IA".
items.answer: The investigation: a clearly structured, analytical argument that answers the research question using evidence from a range of sources (15 marks, about 1,300 words)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the investigation: a clearly structured, analytical argument that answers the research question using evidence from a range of sources (15 marks, about 1,300 words). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why Section 3 should be linked explicitly to the investigation.
items.answer: Generic reflections on history earn few marks; the reflection should draw on specific challenges in the investigation, such as conflicting accounts of the Berlin Airlift, and explain what they reveal about historians’ methods.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Generic reflections on history earn few marks; the reflection should draw on specific challenges in the investigation, such as conflicting accounts of the Berlin Airlift, and explain what they reveal about historians’ methods. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a citation and a bibliography entry.
items.answer: A citation acknowledges a specific source at the point it is used (footnote or in-text); the bibliography lists all sources consulted at the end.
items.markingKey: A citation acknowledges a specific source at the point it is used (footnote or in-text); the bibliography lists all sources consulted at the end. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the relevance of a source and the value of a source.
items.answer: Relevance explains why the source relates to the research question; value is the analysis of how its origin, purpose and content make it useful as evidence for the question.
items.markingKey: Relevance explains why the source relates to the research question; value is the analysis of how its origin, purpose and content make it useful as evidence for the question. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between Section 1 of the IA and Section 2 of the IA.
items.answer: Section 1 identifies and evaluates two sources in depth; Section 2 is the investigation, an argued response to the research question using a range of sources.
items.markingKey: Section 1 identifies and evaluates two sources in depth; Section 2 is the investigation, an argued response to the research question using a range of sources. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between reflection on methods and a summary of findings.
items.answer: Reflection considers how knowledge was produced and its limits; a summary restates what was found.
items.markingKey: Reflection considers how knowledge was produced and its limits; a summary restates what was found. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source A
Footnotes are the historian’s way of showing their workings: they allow readers to check where evidence comes from and to judge how far it supports the argument.
— Anthony Grafton, historian, The Footnote: A Curious History (1997) (paraphrased)

According to Source A, what can be learned about referencing and academic integrity in historical writing? [3]
items.answer: Footnotes show historians’ working; they let readers check evidence; they help judge whether evidence supports the argument.
items.markingKey: Footnotes show historians’ working; they let readers check evidence; they help judge whether evidence supports the argument. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]. Points must be taken from the source; own knowledge is not credited in Question 1.

items.stem:
Source C
The Prime Minister’s letters to his sisters reveal a man convinced that he alone could save the peace. On 3 October 1938 he wrote that “I have been the means of saving the world from war”.
— Robert Self, ed., The Neville Chamberlain Diary Letters, vol. 4 (2005) (paraphrased)

What is the message conveyed by Source C? [2]
items.answer: Chamberlain believed he alone could save peace; he claimed after Munich to have saved the world from war.
items.markingKey: Chamberlain believed he alone could save peace; he claimed after Munich to have saved the world from war. Award 1 mark for each valid point about the message, up to [2]; a description of the source without interpretation of its message scores at most 1.

items.stem:
Source D
I must say that it was a gamble, but it was a gamble that we believed was justified. The Americans had surrounded our country with military bases; now they would learn what it feels like to have enemy missiles pointing at you.
— Nikita Khrushchev, Khrushchev Remembers (1970) (paraphrased)

Outline the message that the author of Source D intended to convey. [2]
items.answer: Khrushchev admitted placing missiles in Cuba was a gamble; he justified it by US bases around the USSR; he wanted the USA to feel threatened as the USSR did.
items.markingKey: Khrushchev admitted placing missiles in Cuba was a gamble; he justified it by US bases around the USSR; he wanted the USA to feel threatened as the USSR did. Award 1 mark for each valid point about the message, up to [2]; a description of the source without interpretation of its message scores at most 1.

items.stem:
Source C
The historian is engaged on a continuous process of moulding his facts to his interpretation and his interpretation to his facts.
— E. H. Carr, What is History? (1961) (extract)

Identify three points made in Source C about the methods used by historians. [3]
items.answer: Historians shape facts to interpretations and interpretations to facts; history is a continuous process of interaction.
items.markingKey: Historians shape facts to interpretations and interpretations to facts; history is a continuous process of interaction. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]. Points must be taken from the source; own knowledge is not credited in Question 1.

items.stem: Outline one way in which an IA flagged for academic misconduct shows the importance of academic integrity.
items.answer: A student copied paragraphs from an online summary of the Korean War without acknowledgement; the work was investigated by the IB. Using unacknowledged material constitutes plagiarism and can lead to no grade being awarded.
items.markingKey: Context (A student copied paragraphs from an online summary of the Korean War without acknowledgement; the work was investigated by the IB.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Using unacknowledged material constitutes plagiarism and can lead to no grade being awarded. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of academic integrity.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that primary sources are always more valuable than secondary sources for a historical investigation.
items.answer: Neither type is inherently more valuable; value depends on the question and the critical use made of the source.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: contemporary perspective and direct evidence; show motives (Chamberlain’s letters); raw material for original analysis. Arguments against: secondary works use many sources and hindsight; primary sources may be propaganda or partial; value depends on the research question. items.stem:
Source D
Kennedy had to balance pressure from his military advisers, who favoured air strikes and invasion, with the risk that any attack would kill Soviet personnel and escalate to nuclear war.
— Sheldon M. Stern, historian at the John F. Kennedy Library, The Week the World Stood Still (2005) (paraphrased)

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source D, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating the Cuban Missile Crisis. [4]
items.answer: Value: Stern studied the ExComm tape recordings in depth, giving an evidence-based account of US decision-making. Limitations: It focuses on the US side and Kennedy’s role, giving less attention to Soviet and Cuban perspectives.
